lead: This unit shows where the converters of Units 2 to 5 are actually used: a UPS under a desk, a charger in a phone, an induction stove, a 2000 MW HVDC link, a solar inverter on a roof. After it you can pick a converter for a given job, size its battery or panel, and work out the ratings, currents and firing angles that decide the design.
about: The unit follows the converters out of the lab and into equipment. Chapter 6.1 takes the UPS, 6.2 the battery charger and emergency lamp, 6.3 induction heating, 6.4 the HVDC link, 6.5 static var compensators and FACTS, 6.6 grid-tied solar and battery storage, 6.7 industrial process control. Each chapter reuses one converter from earlier units and adds the application layer: ratings, control loop, sizing and protection. The early chapters are small stand-alone systems; the later ones scale the same ideas up to a transmission grid and to a plant floor. Sizing sums — backup time, charge time, panel watts, firing angle — run through all seven.

chapters.idea: A UPS keeps a load alive when the mains fails by holding a battery on a DC bus between a charger and an inverter.
chapters.depth: Off-line (standby), line-interactive and on-line (double conversion) topologies with block diagrams; transfer time and the static transfer switch; bypass and maintenance bypass; output waveform, THD and crest factor; VA rating versus watts, load power factor; battery bank sizing and backup time; power supply types (linear, SMPS, UPS) and power conditioners, with the SMPS itself left to Unit 3. Name ferro-resonant and rotary UPS only in one line. Some syllabi call the on-line type 'double conversion' and the off-line type 'standby'.

figure.title: On-line UPS
figure.aria: Mains feeds a rectifier that holds a DC bus with a battery; an inverter feeds the load, and a static bypass can join the load straight to the mains.

chapters.example: A 1 kVA on-line UPS feeds a 640 W load at 0.8 lagging power factor. The battery is 48 V, 100 Ah and the inverter efficiency is 90%. The battery may be taken down to 80% of its capacity. Find the DC current drawn from the battery and the backup time. (Answer: DC power = 640/0.9 = 711 W, current = 711/48 = 14.8 A, usable energy = 48 × 100 × 0.8 = 3840 Wh, backup = 3840/711 = 5.4 h.)
chapters.trap: Multiplying VA by hours and calling it stored energy: apparent power must pass through the load power factor and the inverter efficiency before it becomes battery watts.
chapters.prereq: Unit 3 for the charger stage and SMPS, Unit 4 for the full-bridge inverter and SPWM.
chapters.leave: Modulation and harmonic spectra to Unit 4; cell chemistry and ageing to a battery course.

chapters.idea: A charger is a controlled DC source that follows a charging profile, and the same thyristor or TRIAC switching also runs emergency lamps, dimmers and simple timers.
chapters.depth: Charging methods: trickle, constant current, constant voltage, CC-CV, float versus boost, pulse charging. Charging regulator built from a series pass stage, a buck converter or a flyback, with current-sense and voltage-sense loops and a termination command. Charge factor and charge time; C-rate; temperature and overcharge protection. Emergency lighting: maintained and non-maintained fittings, inverter tube packs, LED emergency drivers, automatic changeover and battery check. Solid-state switching circuits for light dimmers (phase control) and electronic timers (555 or zero-crossing types) in one page each, because Unit 5 owns the switching theory.

figure.aria: Charging a 100 Ah battery at 10 A: current stays flat for 5.6 h, then tapers to 2 A while the voltage rises to 14.4 V and holds.

chapters.example: A 12 V, 100 Ah lead-acid battery is at 50% depth of discharge. It is charged at 0.1C in constant current up to 14.4 V, then held at 14.4 V until the current falls to 2 A. Charge efficiency is 90% and the taper takes 2 h. Find the constant-current time, the total charge time and the charger output power at the start of the constant-voltage stage. (Answer: 0.1C = 10 A; Ah to replace = 50/0.9 = 55.6 Ah; CC time = 5.6 h; total = 7.6 h; CV power = 14.4 × 10 = 144 W.)
chapters.trap: Reading 0.1C as 100 A for a 100 Ah battery, and forgetting that more Ah must be pushed in than were taken out because of charge efficiency.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 for rectifier and filter, Unit 3 for buck and flyback, Unit 5 for the dimmer's phase control.
chapters.leave: TRIAC phase-control waveforms to Unit 5; gassing and cell chemistry to a battery course.

chapters.idea: Induction heating drives a high-frequency current through a coil so that eddy currents and hysteresis inside the workpiece itself make the heat.
chapters.depth: Shorter chapter — only a few universities teach this. Principle and why the heat appears in the metal, not the coil; skin depth δ = √(ρ/(π f μ)) with each symbol defined, and how the working frequency is chosen from it; work coil plus workpiece seen as a transformer with a shorted single-turn secondary; reflected resistance and low power factor; series and parallel load-resonant inverters (link to Unit 3 resonant converters), power control by frequency or by DC link voltage; coupling, Curie point and efficiency. Design steps for a billet or a crucible: power, frequency, turns, coil current, water cooling. Domestic induction cooktops by name only.

figure.title: Induction heating
figure.aria: A DC source feeds a resonant inverter; the coil couples into the workpiece where eddy currents appear, and a control block sets frequency and DC voltage.

chapters.example: A steel billet of diameter 50 mm and length 100 mm is heated from 20 °C to 900 °C in 60 s. Density 7850 kg/m³, specific heat 500 J/(kg·K), overall efficiency 60%, coil voltage 400 V at 0.3 power factor. Find the inverter output power and the coil current. (Answer: volume = 1.963 × 10⁻⁴ m³, mass = 1.54 kg, energy = 1.54 × 500 × 880 = 6.78 × 10⁵ J, metal power = 11.3 kW, inverter power = 11.3/0.6 = 18.8 kW, current = 18800/(400 × 0.3) = 157 A.)
chapters.trap: Using the 50 Hz skin depth for steel; at 10 kHz the depth is a couple of millimetres, which is why the frequency is raised at all.
chapters.prereq: Unit 4 for inverters, Unit 3 for resonant and soft-switched converters, Unit 5 for low-cost cooker circuits.
chapters.leave: Eddy-current field theory and thermal modelling to electromagnetic and heat-transfer courses.

chapters.idea: HVDC sends bulk power as DC between two converter stations, so the line carries no charging current and the power flow is fully controllable.
chapters.depth: Why DC: long overhead lines, undersea cables, asynchronous interconnections, controllability. Line-commutated conversion (LCC) with 12-pulse bridges, converter transformers, AC filters, smoothing reactor, ground electrode; VSC-HVDC with IGBT bridges (link to Unit 4) and its black-start and weak-grid strengths; bipolar and monopolar arrangements with metallic or ground return; reactive power demand of a line-commutated station, about half the DC power; commutation failure in one line; the equations P_d = V_d I_d and the per-pole current; MTDC mentioned only by name.

figure.title: Bipolar HVDC link
figure.aria: AC system A feeds a rectifier station that sends DC along a ±500 kV line to an inverter station, which feeds AC system B; both stations carry filters.

chapters.example: A ±500 kV bipolar HVDC link transmits 2000 MW. Find the DC current in each pole, the power still delivered if one pole trips and the return is through ground, and the reactive power each line-commutated station draws at 50% of DC power. (Answer: V_d pole-to-pole = 1000 kV; I_d = 2000 × 10⁶/1000 × 10³ = 2000 A; monopolar = 500 kV × 2000 A = 1000 MW; Q ≈ 0.5 × 2000 = 1000 MVAr per station.)
chapters.trap: Putting the pole voltage into P = V I for a bipolar link: the DC voltage is the pole-to-pole value, twice the pole-to-ground value.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 for three-phase controlled rectifiers and source inductance, Unit 4 for VSC bridges, Unit 1 for device ratings.
chapters.leave: Converter control loops, harmonic filter design and grid codes to power-system courses.

chapters.idea: SVCs and other FACTS devices switch reactive elements with thyristors fast enough to hold bus voltage and raise the power a line can carry.
chapters.depth: Why vars matter: voltage support and transfer limit. SVC types — thyristor-controlled reactor with fixed capacitor (TCR+FC), thyristor-switched capacitor (TSC), thyristor-switched reactor — and how the firing angle α of the TCR sets the fundamental susceptance B_L(α) = [2(π − α) + sin 2α]/(π X_L). V-I characteristic, control range and rating. STATCOM as a VSC-based compensator with current-source behaviour at low voltage. Series and combined devices named with one line each: TCSC, SSSC, UPFC. Active harmonic filter as a shunt converter that injects the harmonic currents the load draws. SVC at an HVDC terminal to supply the converters' vars.

figure.aria: The FACTS family splits into shunt devices (SVC and STATCOM), series devices (TCSC and SSSC) and the combined UPFC.

chapters.example: A 33 kV bus has a TCR with reactor reactance X_L = 10 Ω per phase at 50 Hz, fired at α = 120°. Using B_L(α) = [2(π − α) + sin 2α]/(π X_L), find the fundamental TCR current per phase and the reactive power absorbed. Repeat for α = 90°. (Answer: σ = π − α = 1.047 rad; B = (2.094 + 0.866)/(π × 10) = 0.0942 S; V_phase = 33/√3 = 19.05 kV; I = 1.79 kA; Q = √3 × 33 × 1.79 = 102 MVAr. At α = 90°, B = 0.1 S, I = 1.905 kA, Q = 109 MVAr.)
chapters.trap: Taking the TCR output as the SVC output: the TCR only absorbs vars, and the fixed capacitor supplies the leading vars, so the net is the difference.
chapters.prereq: Unit 5 for thyristor AC controllers, Unit 4 for VSC-based STATCOM, Unit 2 for converter var demand.
chapters.leave: Stability margin and load-flow studies to power-system courses; filter design to a power-quality course.

chapters.idea: A grid-tied converter is the door between DC sources such as solar and batteries and the AC grid, and its current controller fixes power factor, harmonics and the direction of power.
chapters.depth: PV cell I-V and P-V curves, the maximum power point, and perturb-and-observe MPPT in outline. Single-stage and two-stage grid-tied inverters. Hysteresis current control: the current is kept inside a band around the reference, so switching frequency varies with di/dt; its use for both DC-to-AC and AC-to-DC power flow, and its advantages and disadvantages. Synchronous-link VSI control: real power from the phase shift and reactive power from the voltage difference, written as P = (E V/X) sin δ and Q = (E V cos δ − V²)/X. Rectification at unity power factor, BESS with battery, BMS and power conversion system, and grid services. Sizing of a PV system for home appliances. Anti-islanding and standards named only.

figure.title: Grid-tied PV with storage
figure.aria: A PV array feeds an MPPT boost stage, which holds a DC bus fed also by a battery through a bidirectional converter; a hysteresis-controlled inverter ties the bus to the grid.

chapters.example: A home needs 4 kWh per day. The site gets 4.5 peak sun hours, the system loss factor is 0.75 and the inverter efficiency is 0.9. The battery is 48 V with 2 days of autonomy and 60% depth of discharge. Using 335 Wp panels, find the number of panels and the battery Ah. (Answer: array = 4000/(4.5 × 0.75) = 1185 Wp, so 4 panels = 1340 Wp; daily DC energy = 4000/0.9 = 4444 Wh; storage = 4444 × 2/0.6 = 14 815 Wh; battery = 14815/48 = 309 Ah, choose 300 Ah or 400 Ah.)
chapters.trap: Sizing the array straight from kWh per day, without dividing by peak sun hours and the loss factor, and without the depth of discharge and inverter efficiency on the battery side.
chapters.prereq: Unit 4 for grid-tied inverters and PWM, Unit 3 for boost and bidirectional converters, Unit 2 for power-factor-corrected rectifiers.
chapters.leave: MPPT algorithm detail and islanding detection to specialised courses; modulation to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Process control wraps a feedback loop around a power converter so that one physical variable, such as temperature or level, sits at its set point.
chapters.depth: Shorter chapter — only a few universities teach this. The loop: sensor, transmitter (4–20 mA, thermocouple, RTD), controller (on-off, proportional band, integral, derivative), actuator (thyristor power controller, solid-state relay, contactor, valve), process. On-off versus phase-angle versus integral-cycle control of a heater and the thermal cycling each causes; temperature control of a furnace or oven; liquid level control with a pump or valve; PLC and SCADA in one paragraph with signal isolation. Introduction to AC and DC drives: speed control, V/f control, four-quadrant operation and where drives appear in a plant. Design of a heater control from the load resistance up.

figure.title: Temperature control loop
figure.aria: A set point and a measured oven temperature meet in a PID controller that drives a thyristor power controller, which sets the heater's firing angle.

chapters.example: A 2 kW, 230 V heater is fed through a thyristor AC controller from a 230 V, 50 Hz supply. Find the firing angle and the RMS current for 50% power and for 25% power. Assume a resistive load. (Answer: R = 230²/2000 = 26.45 Ω; 50% power needs V_rms = 230/√2 = 162.6 V at α = 90°, I_rms = 6.15 A. 25% power needs V_rms = 115 V at α ≈ 114°, I_rms = 4.35 A.)
chapters.trap: Treating the controller output in percent as the firing angle: 50% output is α = 90° on a phase-angle controller, but 50% duty cycle on an integral-cycle controller.
chapters.prereq: Unit 5 for AC voltage controllers, Unit 2 for rectifiers feeding DC drives, Unit 3 for DC-DC stages in drive front ends.
chapters.leave: PID tuning theory to control systems; motor modelling and drive dynamics to a drives course.
